findings.description: `two-browser.mjs` checks only that B's print count is unchanged after sending three malformed messages, and its chunk uses an unknown transfer ID that returns before `validChunk` runs. A regression that processes the malformed `need` or mishandles chunks for an active transfer can therefore leave this check green.
findings.title: Malformed transfer messages can pass

findings.description: `AGENTS.md` says nothing received from another device is used until `check.js` accepts it and identifies every network handler as covered by that rule. Existing `dropcheck`, `want`, `have`, and room-message paths consume peer data without a corresponding `check.js` acceptance step, so an agent or reviewer cannot use the stated invariant to assess changes to those paths.
findings.title: The stranger rule describes checks absent

findings.description: `serve.mjs` compares `import.meta.url` with a URL assembled by prefixing raw `process.argv[1]` with `file://`. On Windows, the argument is a backslash-separated drive path rather than the normalized file URL used by `import.meta.url`, so `npm run serve` skips the startup block.
findings.title: Windows users cannot start the server

findings.description: `two-browser.mjs` declares the late-guest check passed when C has two print records, without requesting or checking either file. After A leaves, B can announce metadata and thumbnails to C without transferring full bytes, so the assertion does not establish that C can retrieve the photos B holds.
findings.title: Late guests can lack retrievable files

findings.description: `AGENTS.md` requires work to be queued separately per device and tells reviewers to flag any shared queue. The relay intentionally puts every keyed peer's frames on one page-wide paced queue, so applying this instruction to relay changes would reject the current rate-limiting design without explaining how its shared limit is preserved.
findings.title: The relay rule conflicts with its queue

findings.description: `two-browser.mjs` calls `setWorld` and sends `move` and `dropcheck` directly instead of performing a browser drag. If the canvas pointer handlers stop moving or dropping prints, this transfer check can still pass because the synthetic `dropcheck` starts the receive flow.
findings.title: Broken photo dragging can pass the test
